1:
Against whom the psalm is directed is answered five ways. Augustine of Hippo takes the apostolic citation as decisive: what is written here of another taking the office is prophesied of the betrayer, and Judas in turn represents those who hated Christ then and in their line of succession hate him still. John Calvin makes David a typical character, so that everything expressed must properly be applied to Christ the Head and to all the faithful as his members, while the psalm also shadows forth the destiny of the Jewish nation; he quotes an opinion that the first five verses clearly describe the treatment our Lord met with. John Gill assumes the same throughout, hearing the Messiah as man in every petition. Adam Clarke keeps a primary historical sense and thinks it refers to the counsellor who betrayed David, while allowing a prophecy against Judas; but he adds that if the passages are prophetic it is the Jewish state rather than an individual that is meant. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to identify the man at all: the whole current of the imprecations is turned against one person, but whether it is the Edomite or the Benjamite we do not know; the marks of another hand that raised doubts elsewhere are absent here, and though some expressions look late there are no certain echoes of older models.

Adam Clarke also offers a way of reading the psalm that removes its difficulty altogether. The execrations should be rendered in the future tense, as prophetic denunciations of God’s displeasure against sinners, and taken so they cannot be a stumbling-block to anyone; or else the whole may be the execrations of David’s enemies against himself rather than his against them. On the title given God Charles Ellicott would render it the God of my glory or boast, so that the psalmist prays that the divine silence may not make his confident glorying in the covenant promises vain. Matthew Henry hears an appeal to a judge who saw what the enemies did but seemed to connive at it and keep silence. C.H. Spurgeon notes that only a word is asked for, since a word from God is all a believer needs, and adds that if we take care of God’s honour he will take care of ours.

On the two mouths Charles Ellicott observes that the second word is properly an abstract, of deceit, so that to match them some would read a mouth of wickedness rather than of a wicked man, and the best English is a wicked mouth and a deceitful mouth; he adds a saying that a blow with a word strikes deeper than a blow with a sword, and would render the last clause not spoken against me but talked with me. John Gill catalogues the calumnies as they fell on Christ — that his miracles were done by the devil, that his doctrine was novelty and blasphemy, that he was an enemy to the state — and hears the mouths opened widest at the cross. Adam Clarke keeps it general, that many persons are continually uttering calumnies, and John Wesley notes only that they requite his love with enmity. On the clause our version fills out as giving himself to prayer, both close readers note that the Hebrew says only, and I prayer: Adam Clarke reports the Chaldee’s but I pray, followed by the Greek, Latin and other versions, and Charles Ellicott compares a like compression elsewhere, adding that the context seems to indicate prayer for the enemies themselves.
6:
Whether the adversary of the sixth verse is a person or a common noun divides the entry. Adam Clarke keeps the grammatical meaning: the word means an adversary simply, so the line asks only that the man be opposed and thwarted, though all the versions have devil; . Charles Ellicott agrees and argues from usage, since the same word appears three other times in this psalm in its general sense, which he calls decisive. John Wesley takes the accuser forensically, since standing at the right hand was the place and posture of accusers in the Jewish courts. John Gill and C.H. Spurgeon keep the person: Gill has Judas put into the hands of the one who entered him and put it into his heart to betray his Master, and Spurgeon asks whether the father of lies should not stand near his children. On the wicked ruler C.H. Spurgeon finds the punishment exquisitely just, since no unrighteous man can complain of being governed by one of his own kind.

On the condemnation Charles Ellicott renders it that he may go out of court a condemned man, and refuses to let the next clause mean that his prayer to God is reckoned sin; since the judgment in view is an earthly tribunal, the sense must be that his plea, instead of procuring a mitigation, provokes the unscrupulous judge to make the sentence heavier. Adam Clarke renders the first clause let him come out a wicked man, that is, let his wickedness be made manifest, and quotes a paraphrase to the same effect, that the defence he brings should only deepen his guilt. John Gill moves the scene inward, to the bar of his own conscience, which is as a thousand witnesses.

The eighth verse gave our version a word it could not carry. Adam Clarke says the original means superintendence or oversight, that the common rendering is too technical, and that following the Greek and Latin it has given cause to some light people to be witty, who say the first bishop we read of was bishop Judas. He convicts the witticism easily: the word is used from Genesis downward of offices appointed by God or by his providence, and is applied to Joseph, so one might as well say the first bishop was bishop Joseph — and after all, he adds, Judas was no traitor when he was appointed to his charge among the apostles. Charles Ellicott is content that it means some post of power and influence, and John Gill observes that the days of Judas were few compared with the other apostles, one of whom outlived him by sixty years.

The curse on the children is where Charles Ellicott objects. It is one of the sadly peculiar features of this series that the resentment cannot satisfy itself on the person of the foe but fastens on his innocent descendants, and that a speedy death does not content the imprecator, who must feast his anger on the thought of the fatherless children and the desolate widow. He would render the desolate places as ruins, out of which the children are imagined creeping to beg, and sets beside it a Roman poet’s curse on a husband, that he should live and roam in want through strange towns, exiled and cowering, with no home. Adam Clarke reports the tradition that Judas was married and stole from the bag to support his family. John Gill finds the fulfilment in the dispersion of the Jews after the destruction by the Romans. Matthew Henry distances the psalmist from malice, insisting the imprecation comes not from revenge but from a holy zeal against sin, and reports that Calvin called it a detestable piece of sacrilege, common among friars in his day, to use this psalm as a curse against a neighbour.
11:
Charles Ellicott would render the eleventh verse let the usurer lay traps to catch all that he hath, and sets beside it the curse in the play that prisons should swallow them and debts wither them to nothing. John Wesley notes that the word means to ensnare, so that the taking is by cunning as well as by oppression, and that the stranger has no right to the goods. John Gill supplies two fulfilments — the Romans, who invaded and seized all for the tribute the Jews refused, and Judas, who dying in debt might have left wife and children liable for it — and notes that the Syriac and Arabic render the word creditor.

Adam Clarke makes the fulfilment the whole point. Many of these execrations, he says, were literally accomplished in the case of the Jews after the death of our Lord: expelled from their country, prohibited from returning, and taxed by the Roman government to the lowest degree of poverty. He instances their expulsion from Rome and their settling in a wood outside the Capena gate, where they paid rent for the ground and their whole property was a basket and a little hay, and quotes the satirist who describes them there, in an English version that has every tree paying for its tenant and the Muses expelled from their own grove. On the cutting off of the posterity he adds a second observation of the same kind: the distinction among the tribes is entirely lost, not a Jew in the world knows from which he is sprung, and the royal line survives nowhere but in the person of Jesus.

Why the mother is named beside the father is Charles Ellicott’s question. The sweet of vengeance lies in its completeness, he says, so that the curse must strike backwards as well as forwards and destroy the root with the branch, the form of the imprecation being suggested by the law that visits the iniquity of the fathers on the children; but he asks whether the parallelism alone accounts for the mother, or whether some definite circumstance is in the poet’s thought, and reports that the theory which makes this whole section a quotation of curses actually uttered against David by one of his revilers finds here an allusion to a foreign descent on the mother’s side. John Gill answers the same question by candidates: not the patriarchs, whose failings were forgiven, but either the Amorites and Hittites, called elsewhere the father and mother of the Jews, or their own wicked ancestors who killed the prophets, whose measure of sin was filled up at the crucifixion. On the sins kept continually before the Lord he adds that forgiven sins are cast behind his back or into the depths of the sea, while these are always in sight. Charles Ellicott states the underlying principle plainly: the Hebrew theory of the divine government was that if ruin did not overtake the sinner himself it would fall on his posterity, his name be forgotten and his race extinct.
16:
John Gill lists the failures of mercy the sixteenth verse charges — neither to the poor, nor to the betrayed Master, nor in the priest and Levite who passed by the wounded man, nor in the crowd that answered the sight of the crowned prisoner with a cry for crucifixion. Adam Clarke says that in this case all the dictates of justice and mercy were destroyed, and that on common principles the opposition to Christ cannot be accounted for at all. Charles Ellicott notes that the Hebrew word rendered poor has suggested to some a reference to the murder of a high priest recorded in the later histories. On the love of cursing John Gill and Adam Clarke agree in the same instance, the cry that the blood should be on them and on their children, which Clarke calls an imprecation never more dreadfully fulfilled. John Wesley reads the other half of the verse as a want of delight in desiring and promoting the welfare of others.

The curse worn and drunk draws physiology and travel alike. John Wesley explains the figure medically: water in the cavity of the belly between the bowels is almost certain death, and oil soaking into a bone will soon utterly destroy it. Adam Clarke reports a conjecture that the allusion is to the bitter waters of jealousy that produce a curse, and on the girdle asks that the curse cleave to the man throughout life as a girdle binds the clothes to the body; he then digresses to say that the peoples of the East often wear a gold or silver chain about the waist, and that one such, once the ornament of an officer in the island of Ceylon, lies before him as he writes, silver and curiously wrought. John Gill keeps to the sense, that the man is surrounded on all sides by wrath and that it is as visible as clothing; he notes that one version reads armour rather than garment, as though the cursing were a protection the man imagined he had.

Adam Clarke then proposes that the twentieth verse is the key to everything before it. Rendered fairly, he says, the original gives this is the work of my adversaries before the Lord, and of those who speak evil against my soul — which makes all that stands from the sixth verse to the twentieth the evil words and imprecations of his enemies against him, labouring by their curses to set the Lord against him. This interpretation, he says, frees the whole psalm from every difficulty, since the curses in it are more like those proceeding from the mouth of the wicked than from one inspired by the Spirit of the living God. Charles Ellicott supplies the grammatical ground without drawing the conclusion: the word may mean either work or wages, and the Greek and Latin take the former, giving this is their work who. John Gill keeps the received sense, that this is the just recompense of reward for the hatred shown to Christ.
21:
Charles Ellicott observes that it is almost impossible in English to keep the emphasis of the appeal that opens this section, made the more emphatic by the sudden turn from imprecation on an enemy to prayer for mercy on himself. C.H. Spurgeon notices that the words are very indistinct and that our version, without precisely translating them, hits both the sense and the obscurity; do thou for me leaves the matter open, the psalmist dictating nothing and content that God should undertake for him, and his plea is not his own merit but the name, which the saints have always felt their mightiest argument. Adam Clarke reads it as a direct answer to the preceding curses — while they curse, do thou bless — and takes the verse as a further proof that those curses were the enemies’ own. John Wesley notes only that this mercy is good above the mercy of all the creatures. John Gill hears the prayer of Christ as man, asking that God take his part for his own truth and faithfulness sake.

On the poverty Matthew Henry distinguishes two troubles, the outward condition that gave the enemies their advantage and the wounded heart, which is not merely broken by trouble but wounded with a sense of guilt — and a wounded spirit, he asks, who can bear or heal? John Gill refers the poverty to the circumstances of Christ’s birth and life and chiefly to his helpless estate at his death. On the declining shadow Charles Ellicott explains that as the day declines the shadow lengthens, growing longer and longer until it vanishes in the universal darkness, and that the tossing is better rendered shaken out, as from the lap, the grasshopper being an emblem of timidity. Adam Clarke paraphrases the shadow as having passed the meridian of health and life, and answers the second figure from natural history: when swarms of locusts take wing and the wind blows briskly they are driven upon one another so as to appear heaved to and fro, and a traveller who had seen it said the sight gave a lively idea of the psalmist’s comparison. John Gill prefers the rendering I am made to go, which he takes to mark a violent death.

The weak knees send Adam Clarke to the classics. Hunger, he observes, is felt as soon in weakening the knees as in the stomach, and writers in all countries have noted the effect: he quotes a Greek poet on knees failing, subdued by hunger’s force, in an English version; a Latin comedy in which darkness comes over the eyes and the knees give way for want of food; and a philosophical poem in which the arms and eyelids fall and the knees sink — adding that both the knees and the sight are particularly affected by hunger. John Gill finds the fasting verified in Christ kneeling in the garden, and Charles Ellicott renders the next clause literally, that his flesh has failed him from fat, that is, has dwindled away. On the shaking of the head Adam Clarke gives two instances, the reviler who met David on the road and the passers-by at the cross, and John Gill catalogues the reproaches, that he was called a Samaritan and said to have a devil.
26:
John Gill takes the help asked in the twenty-sixth verse as Christ’s prayer as man, since as a divine person he needed no help but as man was encompassed with infirmities and had help promised him. Adam Clarke asks that the help be so manifest that the enemies see the hand; or, if the words belong to the passion, that they see the sufferer does not suffer on his own account. On the curse and the blessing set against each other John Gill canvasses three renderings — let them curse me, as the reviler cursed David; let them be cursed, with the Syriac; or, with two Jewish commentators, be thou blessed, since if God blesses it matters nothing that wicked men curse. Adam Clarke takes the verse as further proof of the reading he had proposed earlier, that the curses of the psalm are the enemies’ own.

Adam Clarke notes that the shame asked for in the twenty-ninth verse retorts on the adversaries the very figure they had been given earlier, the cursing worn as a garment; Charles Ellicott identifies the mantle as a distinct garment, one worn over the tunic rather than the tunic itself. On the last verse all three voices hear the courtroom of the sixth verse reversed. Charles Ellicott puts it shortest: the Lord is the poor man’s advocate, just as an adversary was the wicked man’s accuser. Adam Clarke extends it: even if the accuser be Satan himself, God will vindicate the innocence of his servant, as when Pilate and the Jews condemned our Lord as a malefactor and God showed his innocence by raising him from the dead; and he records that many understand the whole psalm as referring solely to Christ, the traitor and the wicked Jews. John Gill divides the reference between the Messiah, at whose right hand the Lord stood, and his people, who are poor in every sense and have him as a present help. On the praise promised Adam Clarke hears the confidence of a man who has the fullest prospect of deliverance before him, and of a plenary vindication of his innocence to follow it.
